narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 68.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest factor pushing the model toward predicting failure. Standing in only the second decile, far below the average of roughly sixth-decile performance among accepted students, signaled to the model that you may struggle with the demands of the bar exam. Your first-year ranking in the second decile similarly pulled the prediction in the same direction, reinforcing the concern about consistent academic performance under pressure.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.00 worked in the opposite direction, modestly lowering the predicted risk of failure. However, this positive influence was not strong enough to offset the two class-rank signals.

Taken together, these academic indicators outweighed other details such as your LSAT score of 32, middle-family income background, full-time study plans, gender, and race (none of which were used by the model).

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic trajectory. Consider retaking key courses to raise your GPA, seeking targeted bar-prep support early, or gaining additional professional experience that demonstrates your ability to handle rigorous legal reasoning before reapplying.
